opus-5.5.text:
I think people underrate it because the gains don't show up neatly on the benchmarks everyone watches. When you look at something like a standard eval, you're testing what the model can do with a short prompt, essentially relying on whatever it absorbed during pretraining. But when you give a model a million tokens of context, you're giving it the ability to learn, in a very real sense, at inference time. You can drop in an entire codebase, a whole textbook on a language it's never seen, a huge pile of documentation, and the model gets dramatically better at the task right there in the forward pass.

There was that example where a model was given a grammar and dictionary for a very low-resource language, something with almost no presence on the internet, and it could translate at a level approaching a human who'd studied the same materials. That's a striking thing. It means the model's effective intelligence on a task isn't fixed by its weights; it scales with how much relevant information you can pack into the context.

And the other piece is that in-context learning seems to be remarkably sample efficient, much more so than gradient descent during pretraining. Pretraining needs to see something many, many times to really internalize it. In context, the model can pick up a new pattern or fact from a handful of examples. So if you think about the trajectory toward agents doing long, complex tasks, where they need to hold a lot of state, remember what they tried, understand a large system, long context is a huge part of what makes that feasible. It's kind of like the difference between a smart person walking in off the street versus a smart person who's spent a week reading everything about your project. The second one is just vastly more useful, and I don't think the discourse has fully priced that in.

r001.rationale: The response says long context can make a model better at a task immediately, but it does not identify this as solving the model's onboarding problem.

r002.rationale: It describes giving a model a million-token context containing a codebase and says task performance improves, but does not connect this to next-token prediction or gains associated with increasing model scale.

r003.rationale: It describes supplying large amounts of relevant information, but does not say models can ingest more information than a human or thereby know things their users do not.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing people miss is that context is basically the difference between a model being a very smart person who's just been woken up with amnesia and a very smart person who's actually been working with you for six months. All the intelligence is there in the weights either way, but what you can do with it is wildly different.

So the way I'd frame it is, we've been obsessed with the benchmarks that test the model's stored knowledge, the stuff it absorbed during pretraining. And that's real, that matters. But the thing that makes a colleague useful isn't just that they went to a good school, it's that they know the codebase, they know what you tried last week and why it didn't work, they've read the design doc. A million tokens of context is the model being able to just read the whole codebase, or the whole textbook, or your entire email history, and then reason over it. That's not a marginal improvement, that's a qualitatively different capability.

And the part I think is genuinely underappreciated is that in-context learning is a form of learning. Like, it is actually the model updating on new information. We tend to think of learning as the thing that happens in gradient descent, and then inference is just this frozen thing. But if I show the model a programming language it's never seen, with a grammar reference and a few examples, and it can then write correct programs in that language, in what sense has it not learned it? It's learned it for the duration of that context. And as context gets longer and the models get better at actually using it, as opposed to just nominally having it, that learning gets more and more powerful.

The other piece is that it changes what you can do with the model as a tool. Right now so much of the engineering around these models is retrieval, chunking, summarization, all these hacks to get around the fact that the model can't see everything. A lot of that just goes away. You stop having to guess in advance what's relevant. The model can decide what's relevant, which it's much better at than your retrieval pipeline is.

I think the reason it's underhyped is that it doesn't show up as a big jump on the standard evals. Nobody has a headline number for "can now read the whole repo." But if you actually sit with one of these models and give it a huge amount of context about a real problem, the experience is pretty startling. It feels like a smarter model, even though in some sense it's the same model. And I think that's the tell. If something makes the model feel smarter, it probably is making it smarter, in the way that actually matters for getting work done.

r001.rationale: The response says long context lets a model read a whole codebase and act like a colleague familiar with it, but does not clearly identify instant resolution of the model’s onboarding problem.

r002.rationale: It describes million-token context as a qualitative capability gain, but does not connect it to improved next-token prediction or compare that gain to increases in model scale.

r003.rationale: The response gives examples of large context inputs, but does not say models can ingest more information than a human and thereby know things their users do not.

astra-6.text:
I think people tend to think of context length as a storage feature: you can put a longer PDF in, and the model can answer questions about it. But a lot of intelligence is being able to bring the right information to bear on a problem. A longer context window changes how much information the model can use to figure out what’s going on.

Take working in a new codebase. You could be an excellent programmer, but if someone shows you one function and asks you to fix a bug, you’re going to struggle. You want to see the callers, understand the architecture, look at the tests, and maybe read the discussion that explains why something was implemented that way. Giving a model that context can make it much more capable without changing its underlying weights.

And it opens up a different way of teaching the model. Instead of trying to specify a task perfectly in a paragraph, you can give it lots of examples, including the subtle cases where your preferences are hard to articulate. It can infer what you want from those examples.

The caveat is that fitting information into the window isn’t the same as using it well. Finding a particular sentence in a million tokens is useful, but the more interesting capability is connecting evidence scattered throughout those tokens. If models can do that reliably, then long context starts to look less like a bigger document upload limit and more like the ability to acquire a substantial amount of expertise on the fly.

r001.rationale: The response says codebase context can make a model more capable, but it does not say long context instantly solves the model’s onboarding problem.

r002.rationale: It does not mention millions of tokens, improved next-token prediction, or gains comparable to scaling the model.

r003.rationale: It describes learning from examples and acquiring expertise, but does not say models can ingest more information than humans and thereby know things their users do not.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people tend to think of context length as a convenience feature: you can put a longer PDF in, or you don’t have to split your documents up. But it changes the kinds of problems you can ask a model to solve.

Imagine trying to understand a large codebase when you can only see a few files at a time. Even if you’re a very good programmer, you’re spending a lot of effort figuring out what to look at and keeping track of what you’ve already learned. If you can hold the relevant codebase in context, you can reason about relationships across it much more directly.

There’s also learning from examples. Instead of explaining a task in a paragraph, you could give the model hundreds of examples, including the weird edge cases. That gives it a way to pick up what you actually mean that’s much richer than a short instruction.

The caveat is that fitting information into the context window isn’t the same as using it well. You need the model to connect things that are far apart, distinguish relevant details from distractions, and reason over them. But as that gets better, longer context becomes more than memory. It lets the model bring much more information to bear on a single problem, and that can look like a substantial increase in intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says long context helps understand a codebase more directly, but does not identify instantly solving a model’s onboarding problem as an intelligence gain.

r002.rationale: It discusses holding a codebase in context, but does not state that millions of tokens improve next-token prediction in a way associated with a large increase in model scale.

r003.rationale: The response mentions learning from hundreds of examples, but does not say models can ingest more information than a human and thereby know things users do not.
